title: Your own evidence
hook: keep a simple log: which practice, how you felt

segments.voice: Yesterday: what science can't say. Your line was beyond the lab. Did you ask someone about your question? What did they hear in it? Day three hundred twenty-four.

In his twenties, Benjamin Franklin decided to make himself a better person, systematically. He picked thirteen virtues, temperance, silence, order, and the rest. He ruled a little book into columns, one for each day of the week, and every night he put a small black mark next to any virtue he'd slipped on. He was, he admitted later, surprised to find himself so much fuller of faults than he had imagined. But he could watch the marks thin out. Franklin was running an experiment with a sample of one: himself. Today, as we step out of the lab: your own evidence.
screen: `THIRTEEN VIRTUES, A LITTLE BOOK.` → `A BLACK MARK FOR EVERY SLIP.` → `A SAMPLE OF ONE.`

segments.voice: First, why your own evidence matters. All month we've looked at averages: the median of sixty-six days, a small gratitude effect, a modest boost from compassion training. But you are not an average. The habit study's range ran from eighteen days to hundreds. Some people love slow breathing; some find it makes them anxious. The only way to know what helps you is to watch. Second, keep it simple. A log that's too clever dies by Thursday. Easy beats heroic. One line a day is enough: which practice, how long, and how you felt, maybe on a scale of one to five. After a week or two, look back. Do the days with a walk look different? The days after a late night? Third, be honest about the limits, the way we learned to read a study. Your log isn't a trial. You know what you did, so expectation shapes what you feel. Bad days tend to be followed by better ones no matter what you do, so a practice started on a terrible day will look like a miracle. Look for patterns over weeks, not single days, and hold them loosely. Fourth, the old version. The Stoics did this at night. Seneca describes the philosopher Sextius, whom he admired, who before sleep asked himself: what bad habit have I cured today? What fault have I resisted? In what way am I better? We practiced that evening review in camp three. Franklin's little book was the same thing with columns. Science gave us averages. Your log gives you you. And that closes our two days beyond the lab: the questions only you can answer, and the evidence only you can collect.
screen: `YOU ARE NOT AN AVERAGE.` · `ONE LINE: WHAT, HOW LONG, HOW I FELT.` · `A LOG ISN'T A TRIAL.` · `SENECA'S NIGHT QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `MY OWN DATA.`

segments.voice: Start your log now. On paper or in a note, write today's date. Under it, one line: the practice you did today, how long, and how you feel right now, one to five. That's it. Then sit and let the number be whatever it is. No need to improve it. You're not grading yourself. You're collecting evidence. Plan to add one line each day this week. The bell holds the time.
Your own evidence. A simple daily log of what you practiced and how you felt, read over weeks, with honest limits. Today's word.
Your line: my own data. One line tonight, and one each night for a week: what I did, how long, how I felt. Next week, look back. Day three hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Many people keep a short practice log, one line a day of what they did and how they felt, and review it weekly; the Stoics and later Benjamin Franklin kept nightly self-examinations.

maybe; bad days often bounce back. keep logging.

original.note: Latin: to try, to test; the root of both experience and experiment.

trapdoor: what you thought: evidence is for scientists.
what it means: a simple log of what you did and how you felt, read over weeks.
what a scholar hears: an n-of-1 design, with its known traps: expectation, and regression to the mean after extreme days.

sources.ref: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, part two

notes: Franklin's thirteen virtues and the ruled book with a black mark for each fault: Autobiography, part two (written 1784; plan begun around 1728, when Franklin was about 22). His line 'I was surpris'd to find myself so much fuller of Faults than I had imagined' is paraphrased. Confirm age wording 'in his twenties'.

Seneca, On Anger 3.36: Sextius's nightly questions (what bad habit have you cured today, what fault resisted, in what respect are you better). Review fix: script now says 'the philosopher Sextius, whom he admired' rather than 'a teacher of his', since Seneca studied with Sextius's school, not clearly with Sextius himself. Confirm.
